chunks.title: Getting to Goa
chunks.text: Goa has two airports: Dabolim (GOI) in the south and Manohar International (GOX) at Mopa in the north, which is closer to Anjuna, Vagator and Arambol. Both receive direct domestic flights from Mumbai, Delhi, Bengaluru and Hyderabad, with flying time from Mumbai around one hour. By rail, Madgaon and Thivim are the main stations on the Konkan Railway, and overnight trains from Mumbai take roughly eleven to twelve hours. Pre-paid taxis and app cabs operate from both airports and from Madgaon station. Visitors should note that North Goa and South Goa are around ninety minutes apart by road, so choosing a base close to the intended beaches saves a great deal of transfer time.

chunks.title: When to visit Goa
chunks.text: The peak season runs from mid-November to February, when days are dry, humidity is low and evening temperatures are pleasant. This window includes Christmas and New Year, when accommodation rates rise sharply and must be booked well in advance. March to May is hot and humid but much quieter, with lower room rates and uncrowded beaches. The southwest monsoon arrives in June and continues to September, bringing heavy rain and rough seas; many beach shacks and water sports operators close, although the countryside is green and prices are at their lowest. Shoulder months of October and early November offer a balance of clearing weather and moderate pricing.

chunks.title: What to see in Goa
chunks.text: North Goa centres on the beach belt from Candolim and Calangute through Baga, Anjuna and Vagator to Arambol, with the Saturday night market at Arpora and the Wednesday flea market at Anjuna. Old Goa holds the UNESCO-listed churches and convents, including the Basilica of Bom Jesus and Se Cathedral. Fontainhas in Panaji is the Latin Quarter, best explored on foot for its Portuguese-era houses. South Goa is quieter, with Colva, Benaulim, Palolem and Agonda. Inland, Dudhsagar Falls is most impressive shortly after the monsoon, and the spice plantations near Ponda make a straightforward half-day trip.

chunks.title: Getting around Goa
chunks.text: Scooter and motorcycle hire is the most common way to travel, and a valid driving licence plus helmet is a legal requirement. App-based cabs have limited availability in parts of Goa, and local taxi unions are strong, so fares are often negotiated in advance rather than metered. Pre-booked airport transfers are generally more reliable than arranging a cab on arrival. Kadamba Transport Corporation buses connect the main towns inexpensively but are slow and do not run late. Distances are deceptive: Arambol in the far north to Palolem in the far south is roughly three hours by road, so planning days around one coastal cluster is advisable.

chunks.title: Eating in Goa
chunks.text: Goan cuisine blends Konkan and Portuguese influences. Common dishes include fish curry rice, prawn balchao, chicken or pork xacuti, sorpotel, and the layered bebinca for dessert. Beach shacks serve grilled catch of the day through the dry season, and the fish markets at Panaji and Margao are busiest early in the morning. Feni, distilled from cashew or coconut, is a registered Goan speciality. Vegetarians will find Goan-Hindu thalis widely available inland, particularly around Ponda. Alcohol is taxed at a lower rate than in neighbouring states, which is why dining out is often cheaper than in Mumbai or Bengaluru.

chunks.title: Typical Goa costs
chunks.text: ESTIMATE, per person per day, Indian rupees, excluding flights. Budget travel, using hostels or guest houses and eating at local eateries, is in the region of 1,500 to 2,500. Mid-range travel, with a three-star hotel, a mix of shack and restaurant meals and a hired scooter, runs around 3,500 to 6,000. Higher-end travel using four or five-star resorts and private cabs typically starts near 9,000 and rises steeply over Christmas and New Year, when room rates commonly double or triple. Scooter hire is usually 400 to 700 per day plus fuel, and a one-way North to South Goa taxi transfer is commonly quoted between 2,000 and 3,000.
chunks.cost_basis: ESTIMATE - per person per day, INR, mid-range basis, compiled Oct 2026

chunks.title: Getting to Jaipur
chunks.text: Jaipur International Airport at Sanganer is about twelve kilometres from the city centre and has frequent domestic connections to Delhi, Mumbai and Bengaluru. Jaipur Junction is the main railway station, and several daily trains connect Delhi in roughly four and a half to five and a half hours, including fast morning services. By road, the Delhi to Jaipur stretch of NH-48 takes around five to six hours depending on traffic around Gurugram. Jaipur forms the first point of the Golden Triangle with Delhi and Agra, and many visitors arrive overland as part of that circuit rather than flying directly.

chunks.title: When to visit Jaipur
chunks.text: October to March is the comfortable season, with daytime temperatures generally pleasant and cool evenings in December and January. This is also when the major festivals fall, including Diwali illuminations and the Jaipur Literature Festival in January, both of which push accommodation prices up and fill hotels early. April to June is very hot, with daytime temperatures that make midday sightseeing at exposed forts difficult, though rates drop considerably. The monsoon from July to September brings intermittent rain, cooler air and a green Aravalli landscape, and is a reasonable compromise for travellers who do not mind occasional downpours.

chunks.title: What to see in Jaipur
chunks.text: Amber Fort, about eleven kilometres north of the city, is the principal sight and is best visited early to avoid both heat and crowds. In the walled Pink City are the City Palace, the Jantar Mantar observatory with its UNESCO listing, and Hawa Mahal, whose facade is most photographed from the cafes opposite. Nahargarh Fort offers the clearest view over the city and is popular at sunset, while Jaigarh Fort holds one of the largest wheeled cannons in the world. Jal Mahal sits in Man Sagar lake and is viewed from the shore rather than entered. Shopping concentrates on Johari Bazaar and Bapu Bazaar for textiles, blue pottery and jewellery.

chunks.title: Getting around Jaipur
chunks.text: App-based cabs and auto-rickshaws are widely available and are usually the simplest option for visitors. Auto fares are commonly negotiated rather than metered, so agreeing a price before setting off avoids disputes. Hiring a car with a driver for a full day is a popular choice for covering Amber, Jaigarh and Nahargarh in one circuit, since the forts are spread out and connected by hill roads. The Jaipur Metro covers a limited corridor and is of modest use to tourists. The walled city is compact enough to explore on foot, though traffic is heavy and pavements are inconsistent.

chunks.title: Eating in Jaipur
chunks.text: Rajasthani cuisine is built around dal baati churma, gatte ki sabzi, ker sangri and laal maas, the last being a fiery mutton curry. Jaipur is also known for pyaaz kachori and mirchi vada as street snacks, and for ghewar, a disc-shaped sweet associated with the Teej festival. Lassi served in clay kulhads is a local institution around the old city. Vegetarian food is abundant, and many traditional establishments are entirely vegetarian. Heritage hotels offer Rajasthani thalis in a more formal setting, which is a reliable way to sample several dishes at once.

chunks.title: Typical Jaipur costs
chunks.text: ESTIMATE, per person per day, Indian rupees, excluding transport to the city. Budget travel using hostels and local eateries is in the region of 1,200 to 2,200. Mid-range travel with a three or four-star hotel, paid monument entry and a car with driver for sightseeing days is roughly 3,000 to 5,500. Heritage and luxury hotels start considerably higher and rise during festival weeks. Composite monument tickets covering several sites are generally better value than separate entries, and foreign-national ticket rates are higher than Indian-national rates at most state-run monuments. A full day car with driver is commonly quoted between 2,000 and 3,500.
chunks.cost_basis: ESTIMATE - per person per day, INR, mid-range basis, compiled Oct 2026

chunks.title: Getting to Manali
chunks.text: Manali has no airport of its own. The nearest is Bhuntar (KUU) near Kullu, about fifty kilometres away, with limited and weather-dependent flights. Most visitors travel overland from Delhi, a distance of roughly 530 kilometres, taking twelve to fourteen hours by overnight Volvo coach or private car. Chandigarh is a common alternative starting point at around eight to nine hours. The nearest broad-gauge railhead is Chandigarh, with Joginder Nagar on a narrow-gauge line being closer but slower. The Atal Tunnel has substantially shortened the onward journey to Lahaul and Spiti, making Sissu and Keylong feasible as day trips in season.

chunks.title: When to visit Manali
chunks.text: March to June is the main season, with clear mountain views, open high passes from late May and comfortable daytime temperatures. July to early September brings monsoon rain, and landslides can close sections of the Chandigarh to Manali highway at short notice, so buffer days are sensible. October and November are crisp and quiet with excellent visibility. December to February brings snow, which is the main draw for many visitors, though Rohtang Pass is generally closed and road access can be interrupted. Permits are required for Rohtang Pass and are capped daily, so arranging them in advance through a registered operator matters during the busy months.

chunks.title: What to see around Manali
chunks.text: Old Manali is the backpacker quarter, with cafes along a steep lane above the Manalsu stream. Hadimba Devi Temple sits in a deodar grove a short walk from the Mall Road, and Vashisht has hot springs and a temple complex. Solang Valley, about thirteen kilometres north, is the main activity area for paragliding, zorbing and winter snow sports. Rohtang Pass, subject to permits and weather, is the classic high-altitude excursion, while the Atal Tunnel gives easier access to Sissu waterfall and the Lahaul valley. Naggar Castle and the Roerich Gallery, south of town, make a quieter half-day outing.

chunks.title: Getting around Manali
chunks.text: The town centre around Mall Road is walkable, and Old Manali is a steep twenty to thirty minute walk or a short auto ride. For Solang, Rohtang and the Atal Tunnel, shared taxis and private cabs operate from the taxi stand at fixed union rates, and vehicles are often specified by type because of the gradients. Local buses run to Vashisht, Naggar and Kullu inexpensively. Self-drive scooters are available but are not advisable in snow or heavy rain. During peak snow, chains or four-wheel drive may be required beyond Solang, and operators will refuse to proceed if conditions are unsafe.

chunks.title: Eating in Manali
chunks.text: Himachali dishes include siddu, a steamed stuffed bread usually served with ghee, as well as chana madra and the multi-course dham served at ceremonial occasions. Trout from the Beas and from local farms appears on many menus. Old Manali has a long-established cafe culture with Israeli, Tibetan and continental menus alongside Indian food, reflecting decades of backpacker traffic. Tibetan momos and thukpa are widely available and inexpensive. At altitude, visitors are generally advised to eat lightly on the first day and to keep fluid intake up.

chunks.title: Typical Manali costs
chunks.text: ESTIMATE, per person per day, Indian rupees, excluding travel from Delhi or Chandigarh. Budget travel using hostels in Old Manali and local dhabas is in the region of 1,200 to 2,000. Mid-range travel with a comfortable hotel, a shared cab for sightseeing and paid activities is roughly 2,800 to 5,000. Resorts and premium properties sit higher, and rates rise sharply around Christmas, New Year and the summer school holidays. A Delhi to Manali Volvo coach seat is commonly in the 1,200 to 2,200 range one way, a Solang day cab around 2,000 to 3,000, and paragliding is typically quoted from about 1,500 for a short flight.

chunks.title: Getting to Alleppey and Munnar
chunks.text: Cochin International Airport (COK) is the usual entry point, with Alleppey about eighty-five kilometres away by road and Munnar around 110 kilometres, each roughly three to four hours depending on traffic and ghat conditions. Trivandrum (TRV) is an alternative for southern Kerala. Alappuzha has its own railway station on the coastal line, with direct services from Ernakulam and Trivandrum. Munnar has no railhead, and the nearest practical station is Aluva. A common routing is to fly into Kochi, spend a night in Fort Kochi, continue to Munnar for the hills and finish in the backwaters at Alleppey before departing.

chunks.title: When to visit Alleppey and Munnar
chunks.text: September to March is the most comfortable period, with lower humidity and reliable sunshine. December and January are the busiest and most expensive, especially for houseboats. The southwest monsoon from June to August brings heavy rain; houseboat cruising continues but views are limited, and this is the traditional season for Ayurvedic treatment, when many resorts offer lower rates. Munnar is noticeably cooler than the coast year-round and can be misty at any time. The Nehru Trophy snake boat race at Alappuzha is usually held in the monsoon months and fills accommodation in the town when it takes place.

chunks.title: What to see in Alleppey and Munnar
chunks.text: The Alleppey backwaters are the main attraction, experienced either on an overnight houseboat or on a cheaper shikara for a few hours. The state-run ferry between Alappuzha and Kottayam is an inexpensive alternative that locals use. Munnar is a tea landscape: the Tata Tea Museum explains processing, Eravikulam National Park protects the Nilgiri tahr and is closed during the calving season, and viewpoints at Top Station and Echo Point are the usual stops. Mattupetty Dam and the surrounding plantations fill a half day. Fort Kochi, on the way, holds the Chinese fishing nets, St Francis Church and the Mattancherry synagogue.

chunks.title: Getting around Kerala
chunks.text: Hiring a car with a driver for several days is the most common arrangement, since the Kochi-Munnar-Alleppey circuit involves long ghat drives that are tiring to self-drive. State buses are frequent and very cheap between major towns, but slow. In Alappuzha, shikara boats are hired by the hour from the boat jetty, and houseboats normally board around midday and disembark the following morning. Autos are available in both towns and fares are usually negotiated. Munnar's viewpoints are spread over considerable distances along winding roads, so a day cab is generally more practical than piecing together local transport.

chunks.title: Eating in Kerala
chunks.text: The Kerala sadya is a vegetarian banquet served on a banana leaf, traditionally at Onam and widely available at lunch. Coastal cooking features karimeen pollichathu, prawn and fish moilee in coconut milk, and appam with stew. Puttu with kadala curry is a common breakfast, as is idiyappam. Toddy shops inland serve strongly spiced food alongside fermented palm sap and are an authentic if unpolished experience. Houseboat packages normally include meals cooked on board, often featuring the day's catch, and dietary requirements are usually accommodated if notified at booking.

chunks.title: Typical Kerala costs
chunks.text: ESTIMATE, per person per day, Indian rupees, excluding flights. Budget travel using homestays and local restaurants is in the region of 1,500 to 2,500. Mid-range travel with comfortable hotels, a car with driver shared between two, and one houseboat night is roughly 4,000 to 7,000. Premium resorts and luxury houseboats sit considerably higher. An overnight houseboat for two, including meals, is commonly quoted between 8,000 and 15,000 for the boat in regular season and rises substantially between late December and early January. A shikara hire is typically 600 to 1,200 per hour, and a Kochi to Munnar one-way cab around 3,000 to 4,500.

chunks.title: Getting to Rishikesh
chunks.text: Dehradun's Jolly Grant Airport (DED) is about twenty kilometres away and is the nearest air link, with direct flights from Delhi and several other cities. Haridwar Junction is the usual railhead, roughly forty-five minutes by road, and Rishikesh has a smaller station with limited services. By road from Delhi the distance is around 240 kilometres, taking five to seven hours depending on traffic through Meerut and Muzaffarnagar, and overnight buses are frequent. Many visitors combine Rishikesh with Haridwar, which is close enough to visit for the evening Ganga Aarti and return the same night.

chunks.title: When to visit Rishikesh
chunks.text: September to November and February to May are the strongest windows. River rafting season generally runs from late September to the end of June and is suspended during the monsoon for safety reasons, so July and August visitors should not expect to raft. Summer months from April to June are warm but remain pleasant by the river and are busy with domestic visitors. Winter is cold in the mornings and evenings but clear, and the ashrams are quieter. The International Yoga Festival is usually held in March and fills accommodation in the Tapovan and Swarg Ashram areas.

chunks.title: What to see in Rishikesh
chunks.text: Lakshman Jhula and Ram Jhula are the suspension bridges that define the layout of the town, with Tapovan on one bank and Swarg Ashram on the other. Triveni Ghat holds the evening Ganga Aarti, which is less commercial than the equivalent at Haridwar. The Beatles Ashram, formally Chaurasi Kutia, is now a ticketed site within Rajaji Tiger Reserve with graffitied meditation huts. Neelkanth Mahadev Temple is a longer excursion into the hills. Rafting put-ins at Shivpuri and Brahmapuri serve the standard sixteen and twenty-six kilometre stretches, and the waterfall walks near Neer Garh are a short trip from town.

chunks.title: Getting around Rishikesh
chunks.text: The core areas are walkable, and crossing between banks is on foot over the suspension bridges, which do not take cars. Shared autos run along the main roads from the bus stand to Lakshman Jhula and Tapovan at low fixed fares, and private autos are available for direct trips. Scooter hire is common for reaching Neelkanth and the waterfalls. Rafting operators usually include the upstream transfer in the package price, returning participants to a point near town at the end of the run. Note that Rishikesh is a vegetarian and alcohol-free town by regulation, which also shapes what is available near the ghats.

chunks.title: Eating in Rishikesh
chunks.text: Rishikesh is officially vegetarian, and alcohol is prohibited, so the food scene is built around vegetarian and vegan cooking. Cafes in Tapovan and around Lakshman Jhula serve extensive multi-cuisine menus aimed at long-staying visitors, including Israeli, Italian and health-food options alongside North Indian standards. Ashrams provide simple sattvic meals, often at fixed hours and included in stay charges. Street food centres on chole bhature, aloo puri and local sweets. Filtered or bottled water is advisable, and many cafes advertise their filtration arrangements.

chunks.title: Typical Rishikesh costs
chunks.text: ESTIMATE, per person per day, Indian rupees, excluding travel from Delhi. Budget travel using hostels or basic ashram accommodation and eating locally is in the region of 900 to 1,800, making Rishikesh one of the cheaper destinations in this set. Mid-range travel with a riverside hotel, cafe meals and one or two paid activities is roughly 2,500 to 4,500. Premium camps and wellness resorts sit well above this. A sixteen-kilometre rafting run is commonly quoted between 600 and 1,200 per person, bungee jumping around 3,500 to 4,000, and a multi-day yoga teacher training course runs into tens of thousands depending on the school and duration.
